4. Observations and Recommendations on the Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber 
Security) Rules, 2024 and Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure) Rules, 2024  
Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024 
4.1 The Committee notes that Rule 2(e) defines a "securi ty incident" as "an event having 
real or potential risk on telecom cyber security."  On concerns that this definition is overly 
broad and whether it aligns with existing definitions, such as those under CERT -In or global 
standards, the Department of Telecom (DoT) has informed, with examples of such definitions 
from the National Institute of Standards and Technology USA and the Ministry of Electronics 
and Information Technology (MeitY) Notification dated 29.04.2016, that the definition aligns 
with global best  practices and is necessitated by the DoT’s new responsibility for telecom 
network security under the Allocation of Business Rules. Taking note of the submissions, 
the Committee supports the broad definition of a "security incident" under Rule 2(e), as 
a n ecessary measure to safeguard critical telecom infrastructure; however, to address 
concerns about its scope and ensure practical implementation, the Committee observes 
that the DoT may consider refining the definition, and may evaluate it for introducing a 
tiered incident classification system to prioritize reporting of major incidents, ensuring a 
balanced approach to telecom cybersecurity. 
4.2 The Committee , in context of suggestions, to include Virtual Telecom Network 
providers also in the definition unde r the Rules 2(f)  notes that in its submissions ,  the 
Department has clarified that under Rule 2(f), which defines a "telecommunication entity" , 
the definition already encompasses Virtual Telecom Network Providers (VTNPs), as it 
includes any person providi ng telecommunication services or operating a telecommunication 
network, specifically covering authorized entities under the Telecommunications Act, 2023.  
Noting the clarification, the Committee observes that the Department may apprise the 
TSPs in this regard also.  
4.3 The Committee notes under Rule 2(1)(g), the definition of "telecommunication entity" 
has been given. The Committee is of the view that in order to enhance consistency and clarity 
in the said rules the term be suitably defined to explicitly distinguish it from 
"telecommunication service provider"  (TSP). The Committee observes that the current 
definition in Rule 2(1)(g) is broad, encompassing both service providers and network 
operators, which risks inconsistent application. The Committee recommends that 
suitable necessary action in this regard be taken by the Department of Telecom. 
15 

4.4 The Committee notes the provisions of Rule 3(1)(a) which allow for seeking, from  a 
telecommunication entity, traffic data and any other data, other than content of messages, in 
the form and manner as may be specif ied by the Central Government on the portal .  The 
Committee in this respect observes that the wording “any other data" under this Rule is quite 
broad in scope and can raises potential for privacy violations. In this regard the Committee 
recommends that the Department should explicitly define the categories of data 
permissible for collection, limiting it to what is strictly necessary for telecom 
cybersecurity.  
4.5 The Committee notes that Rule 3(2)(b) permit the Government  to analyse collected 
traffic data for enhancing telecom cybersecurity and share such analysis with 
telecommunication entities or users as deemed necessary. On the aspect of clarity regarding 
the scope of data to be shared and the circumstanc es for sharing, the Department has clarified 
that the rule pertains to sharing analysis derived from data, not the raw data itself, and that 
sharing with telecommunication entities or users is necessary to enable corrective actions to 
ensure cybersecurity,  such as notifying a user or entity about a targeted threat. The 
Committee observes that telecommunication entities, as network operators, and users, as 
end-points, play a vital role in implementing corrective measures, justifying their 
inclusion in the da ta-sharing framework. The Committee, however recommends that a 
mechanism of having a periodic review of the data -sharing framework to assess its 
effectiveness in enhancing telecom cybersecurity and address emerging privacy or 
security challenges  be set up. Besides efforts towards regular engagement with 
stakeholders regarding the sharing process and evolving cybersecurity standards shall 
also be beneficial. 
4.6 The Committee takes note of the provisions of Rule 3(3) wherein it is stated that the 
Central Government and any agency authorized by the Central Government to collect data 
under these rules, as well as persons with whom such data is shared under sub -rule (2), shall 
put in place adequate safeguards, including any specific safeguards as may be specified by the 
Central Government to ensure that such data is stored and maintained in strict confidentiality 
and prevent any unauthorized access thereto. In this regard, the Committee is of the view 
that the phrase "adequate safeguards" is vague and fails to elaborate upon what level of 
safeguards will be considered adequate. Thus, the Committee recommends that t o 
provide clarity on the term "adequate safeguards”, the Department should issue 
detailed guidelines specifying mandatory technical and proce dural measures for 
authorised agencies and telecom entities.  
16 

4.7 The Committee notes that Rule 4(2)  (b), prohibits telecommunication entities from 
transmitting any message that is fraudulent. The Committee observes that the term 
"fraudulent" is too broad, lacks a clear definition within the rule, and raises concerns about 
who determines whether a message is fraudulent, noting that innocent individuals may 
unknowingly forward such messages. In view of this, the Committee recommends that to 
address concerns about the broadness of the term "fraudulent" and risks to innocent 
senders, the DoT may take necessary ac tion to explicitly define the term, establish clear 
criteria and processes for determining fraudulence, and provide robust support for 
telecommunication entities and users in this regard.  
4.8 The Committee notes that Rule 4(4)(a) mandates that every telec ommunication entity 
should adopt a telecom cybersecurity policy. Upon noting that the Telecom Service Providers 
(TSPs) are already required under extant license conditions to maintain an "organizational 
policy on security and security management of their networks”, the Committee had queried as 
to whether this requirement imposes an unnecessary compliance burden and cost on TSPs. In 
their submission, the Department has stated that these Rules are applicable to a broader range 
of telecom entities, including t hose exempt from authorization, and that the rule does not 
create additional burdens for licensees already complying with similar license conditions. The 
Committee observes that a standardized cybersecurity policy is essential to address 
evolving threats a nd ensure that all entities, licensed or otherwise, maintain robust 
security practices. Thus, the Committee agrees with the laid requirement for all 
telecommunication entities to adopt a telecom cybersecurity policy, as it strengthens the 
security across a diverse ecosystem.  
4.9 The Committee in respect of Rule 4(4)(f) observes that it mandates telecommunication 
entities to conduct periodic cybersecurity  audits, both internally and through certified 
agencies, and share audit reports with the Government. The Department in this respect has 
submitted that Telecom Service Providers (TSPs) already comply with such requirements 
under the National Security Direc tive on Telecommunications Sector (NSDTS), Mandatory 
Testing and Certification of Telecom Equipment (MTCTE), and COMSEC, as well as internal 
audits and periodic audits by DoT’s Licensed Service Area (LSA) units. Further the 
Department has informed that it has taken steps to streamline audits by standardizing 
proformas and automating workflows, and has mentioned that this is an ongoing process. The 
Committee observes that framing clear guidelines on scope and frequency, by the DoT 
shall be helpful in ensurin g that the cybersecurity objectives are readily met by the 
TSPs.  
17 

4.10 The Committee notes that in its submissions on Rule 4(4)(h)(vi) which mandates 
telecommunication entities to maintain records or logs for a period specified by the Central 
Government and make them available to authorized agencies or persons, it has been informed 
that the maximum duration will be determined through consultations with stakeholders, 
including Telecom Service Providers (TSPs), Internet Service Providers (ISPs), the Chief 
Information Security Officer (CISO) of DoT, and the country’s security apparatus. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends that inclusive stakeholder consultations be 
conducted so that a practical, secure, and effective log retention framework, which 
minimizes burden on telecommunication entities gets framed at the earliest.  
4.11 The Committee takes note of Rule 5(5)(a) which authorizes the Government to 
temporarily suspend the use of a telecommunication identifier for a duration specified in an 
“Order”. Upon the question to specify the duration of suspension and propose a maximum 
timeline of 30 days, the Department of Telecom (DoT) has submitted that users will receive 
notice and an opportunity to respond before suspension, and the duration will be determ ined 
on a case-by-case basis mentioning that fixing a uniform 30 -day limit may be impractical due 
to the variable time required for investigations by law enforcement agencies. The Committee 
while taking note of the submission observes that for cases requir ing longer suspensions 
(e.g., complex investigations by law enforcement), the DoT should allow extensions 
through a formal process, like clearly stating the reasons for such extension and also 
giving a tentative resolution timeline. 
4.12 Rule 6 regarding Chief Telecommunication Security Officer  (CTSO) states that 
“Every telecommunication entity shall appoint a Chief Telecommunication Security Officer, 
whose details shall be provided in writing to the Central Government in the form as may be 
specified on th e portal and any replacement or change of such officer shall be promptly 
intimated to the Central Government, in such form as may be specified on the portal by that 
Government”. The Committee notes  that as per the extant license conditions, TSPs are 
already required to appoint a ‘Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). On the question of 
if  there is an overlap in the responsibilities of the CISO and CTSO, the Department has 
mentioned that as per the license condition “39.23 (i) The Chief Officer in char ge of technical 
network operations and the Chief Security Officer/Chief Information Security Officer, and in -
charge of GMSC, MSC, Soft -Switch, Central Database, ILD Gateway, VSAT Hub, INSAT 
MSS-R Hub, PMRTS Central/Base Station, GMPCS Gateway, Switches and  System 
Administrators shall be resident Indian citizen.” and thus the Chief security officer has been  
18 
 

re-designated as Chief Telecommunication Security officer along with its responsibilities in 
the extant rules and thus no additional responsibility has been cast. The Committee notes the 
clarification given. 
4.13 The Committee notes that Rule 7(2) allows the Government  to disclose security 
incidents to the public or require affected telecommunication entities to do so when deemed in 
the public interest. The Committee agrees with the provision, for public disclosure of 
security incidents, as it supports cybersecurity awa reness and public safety besides 
educating the public about cybersecurity trends, enhance awareness, and prevent future 
incidents. However, the Committee observes that to address concerns about unnecessary 
panic and reputational loss of the telecommunicati on entity, the DoT should issue clear 
guidelines on disclosure circumstances, prioritize direct notifications to affected persons, 
and implement safeguards to protect privacy and manage public perception.  
4.14 The Committee notes that under Rule 10 , as a positive step towards Digital 
implementation of the Rules, establishment of a centralized portal has been stated for 
compliance and reporting streamlining obligations. The Committee observes that the 
success of the portal shall depend on accessibilit y, security, and effective 
implementation. The Committee recommends that the portal’s development be 
expedited and all steps be taken to ensure that it is secure, user -friendly, and supported 
by clear guidelines.  
4.15 The Committee observes that the absence of mandatory malware testing for devices 
such as mobile phones, servers, and smart watches poses a significant cybersecurity risk to 
India’s telecom ecosystem. These devices, integral to telecom networks, can harbour 
malware, spyware, or other vulnerabi lities that compromise data integrity, network security, 
and national security. The Committee further observes that addressing this gap is critical to 
prevent malicious software from infiltrating telecom networks and critical infrastructure. The 
Committee, therefore recommends that suitable steps be taken towards enforcing 
malware testing, strengthening supply chain security, and promoting indigenous 
solutions, so that the country’s telecom networks can be safeguarded from malicious 
threats.  
4.16 The Committee taking note of the newer emerging technologies is of the view , that 
integrating Post -Quantum Cryptography (PQC) into India’s telecom networks is critical to 
counter future quantum-based threats and provide a robust foundation for this transition.  
19 
 

In this regard, the Committee recommends that to secure telecom networks against 
quantum-based attacks, a strategic, phased adoption of Post-Quantum Cryptography  
(PQC) should be implemented as its integration is essential to ensure long-term security. 
Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 2024  
4.17 The Committee notes that Rule 4 mandates that spares, hardware, and software used in 
CTI comply with specified standards.  The Committee also takes note that the Department of  
Telecom in its submission has emphasized the critical role of spares in maintaining telecom 
infrastructure and has justified their inclusion in the CTI framework as a security requirement, 
asserting that it does not increase the compliance burden on Telec om Service Providers 
(TSPs). It has also been submitted that spares are essential for the maintenance and 
operational continuity of CTI and as spares replace failed equipment, they must adhere to the 
same standards to ensure network reliability and securit y. The Committee observes that 
substandard spares could introduce vulnerabilities, compromising the integrity of 
critical infrastructure and thus mandating compliance for spares is a prudent measure 
to safeguard national security and public interest. Howev er, the Committee also 
observes that smaller TSPs, in particular, may face challenges in sourcing compliant 
spares, especially if supply chains are limited or if compliant spares are costlier. Thus, 
while supporting the inclusion of spares in the CTI  Rules, 2024, as a critical security 
measure, the Committee recommends that the Department of Telecom may adopt a 
balanced approach through clear guidelines, phased implementation, and targeted 
support for smaller operators as these measures will strengthen the telecom 
infrastructure's resilience while fostering a conducive environment for compliance. 
4.18 The Committee notes that Rule 5(1) authorizes the Government to inspect hardware, 
software, and data related to CTI and in this respect,  it has been informed that such 
inspections are an extension of existing field inspections conducted by DoT units to ensure 
compliance by telecom entities. The Committee also notes that it has been submitted that 
security incidents will follow standard pro cesses, including reporting and mitigation. The 
Committee is of the view that such inspections enable proactive identification of 
vulnerabilities or non -compliance, and thereby reduces the risk of disruptions or 
cyberattacks on critical telecom infrastruct ure. Thus, the Committee endorses the 
inspection provisions under the Rules, as a critical mechanism to ensure compliance and 
security of telecom infrastructure. However, the Committee recommends that to 
enhance effectiveness and address concerns about ope rational disruptions, the DoT 
should adopt a hybrid inspection framework combining routine and incident-triggered  
20 

inspections, supported by clear guidelines, standardized protocols, and stakeholder 
engagement. The Committee feels that these measures wi ll strengthen the security of 
CTI while fostering a collaborative and efficient compliance environment for telecom 
entities. 
4.19 The Committee notes that Rule 6(2)(h) mandates that all logs related to CTI be 
provided to assist in real -time anomaly detecti on and intelligence generation by the 
Government. The Committee notes that it has been informed that real -time log submission is 
essential for proactive security monitoring through a Security Operation Center (SOC). The 
Committee understands that logs are indispensable for post -incident analysis and that 
real-time access would be helpful in preventing or mitigating large-scale cyber incidents; 
however, the Committee also notes that continuous log submission may undermine the 
proactive monitoring capabilitie s leading to delays in the detection of emerging threats 
and a balanced approach needs to be developed. Taking note of the requirements of 
real-time log submission, the Committee recommends all steps be taken to ensure that 
the SOC infrastructure can handle large volumes of logs without compromising 
performance or security. Also, all steps to ensure that SOC infrastructure is fortified 
against cyberattacks through regular security assessments and compliance with global 
cybersecurity standards be taken. 
4.20 The Committee notes that Rule 7(b) places an obligation on the Telecommunication 
entity to maintain a complete list of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure. The 
Committee further notes that it their submissions, the Department has clarified that the list of 
Critical Telecom Infrastructure (CTI) s hall be finalized in consultation with respective 
operators (authorized entities/licensees). The Committee appreciates the approach and the 
clarification given and observes that since Telecom operators possess detailed knowledge 
of their infrastructure, including its technical specifications, operational significance, 
and vulnerabilities , finalizing the CTI list in consultation with respective operators is 
both a practical and strategic necessity. 
4.21 The Committee takes note that the Rule 7(1)(e) mandates Telecom Service Providers 
(TSPs) to maintain and provide supply chain records for telecommunication equipment 
deployed in CTI. The Committee also notes that supply chain details are considered 
confidential by Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and are already submitted to the 
Government through the National Security Directive on Telecommunications Sector 
(NSDTS) and the Mandatory Testing and Certification of Telecom Equipment (MTCTE) 
program. On the query raised as to why these submissions cannot be utilized to reduce the  
21 

compliance burden on TSPs, the Department of Telecom (DoT) has informed that NSDTS 
captures supply chain details only for equipment deployed after 15.06.2021, and MTCTE 
lacks provisions for supply chain records, necessitating the rule to ensure comprehensive 
visibility at a single point. In view of the stated information, the Committee endorses the 
requirement under Rule 7(1)(e), to maintain supply chain records as a critical m easure 
to ensure the security of critical telecom infrastructure; however, to reduce the 
compliance burden on TSPs and enhance efficiency, the Committee recommends that 
DoT should make efforts to integrate NSDTS data and adopt a phased approach for 
legacy equipment, and also provide robust support to TSPs. in case they face any issue 
in providing the data sought.  
4.22 The Committee taking note of the Rule 7(1)(j) observes that it mandates Telecom 
Service Providers (TSPs) to report security incidents to the  Central Government within six 
hours of their occurrence. Also, the Committee observes that under Rule 7(1) of the Telecom 
Cyber Security Rules,  2024 regarding reporting of Security Incidents, it has been stated that 
“The telecommunication entity shall –) within six hours of becoming aware of a security 
incident affecting its telecommunication network or telecommunication service, report the 
same to the Central Government with relevant details of the affected system including the 
incident”. Detailed report will then be required within 24 hours.   The Committee also notes 
that the extant CERT -In guidelines require reporting within six hours of becoming aware of 
an incident. The Committee while observing that the CTI -specific incident reporting 
requirement is a  necessary measure to enhance the security of critical telecom infrastructure 
also notes that with the six -hour timeline triggered from the “occurrence” of an incident, as 
opposed to CERT -In’s “awareness” trigger, a practical challenge also emerges as TSPs  may 
not immediately detect incidents due to their complexity or latency in monitoring systems, 
rendering the “occurrence” timeline unrealistic. Taking it in view, the Committee 
recommends that to improve practicality and reduce the compliance burden, the DoT 
may consider aligning the reporting timeline with CERT - In’s “awareness” trigger, 
streamline reporting processes to avoid duplication, and provide robust support to 
TSPs. The Committee also notes that this shall bring similarity in provisions in both t he 
Rules.  
4.23 The Committee notes that Rule 8(8) exempts routine software updates aimed at 
incrementally improving the performance or security of CTI from certain regulatory 
requirements. In this respect, the Department has submitted that routine software updates, 
deployed by Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), address shortcomings and  
22 
 

vulnerabilities to ensure stable operation and enhance CTI performance and security, and are 
therefore exempted under the rule. However, the Committee observes that without a 
precise definition, there is a risk of ambiguity, potentially allowing non -routine or 
significant updates to be misclassified as routine, bypassing necessary oversight, or 
causing confusion among Telecom Service Providers (TSPs) and OEMs about 
compliance requ irements. Thus, the Committee recommends that in order to address 
concerns about ambiguity, the DoT should clarify and clearly define "routine software 
update,” with defined criteria and guidelines so that TSPs and OEMs stand in 
compliance. 
4.24 The Commit tee notes that a significant portion of India’s telecom network 
infrastructure potentially relies on equipment from Chinese manufacturers, raising critical 
cybersecurity and national security concerns due to the risk of embedded vulnerabilities, 
backdoors, or unauthorized data access. These risks are particularly acute given the borderless 
nature of cyber threats and the strategic importance of telecom networks as critical 
infrastructure. The Committee observes that though the Critical Telecom Infrastructur e 
and Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024, provide a robust framework to address these 
concerns, but targeted actions are needed to mitigate the specific risks posed by foreign, 
particularly Chinese-made, equipment. In this regard, the Committee recommends that 
to address the security risks associated with such telecom equipment, a phased "Rip -
and-Replace" strategy should be implemented. Further this strategy could involve 
systematically identifying, removing, and replacing high -risk equipment with trusted, 
preferably indigenous, alternatives while strengthening supply chain security and 
enforcement mechanisms. This shall also allow India  to position itself as a global leader 
in secure telecom manufacturing.  
4.25 The Committee observes that the compliance provisions under the Critical Telecom 
Infrastructure Rules, 2024, may impose additional responsibilities on Telecom Service 
Providers (TSPs) to ensure national security and maintain critical telecom infrastructure . In 
respect of the query as to whether the costs of compliance should be reimbursed by the 
Government, the Department has submitted that these costs are inherent to the operational and 
business obligations of TSPs, as outlined in existing license conditio ns. It has further been 
submitted that compliance with security requirements is a fundamental aspect of operating in 
the telecom sector, and such costs should be factored into TSPs' business plans besides the 
security obligations vary by country due to dif fering security environments and regulatory 
frameworks. The Committee observes that there are instances where in some countries,  
23 
 

regulators provide financial compensation or cost -sharing mechanisms to TSPs for 
compliance with national security -related infrastructure mandates. In view of the 
foregoing, the Committee recommends that the Government may assess the actual cost 
implications of the se Rules and if required, may consider a hybrid approach in this 
regard or may consider offering incentives, such as tax breaks or subsidies, for 
compliance costs specifically tied to new mandates under the Rules. 
4.26 The Committee takes note of the submis sions by the Department of Telecom on the 
aspect of Cyber Security and National Security Issues arising from Mobile Phones that it 
cannot take action regarding mobile phones as they were denotified from the Mandatory 
Testing and Certification of Telecom Eq uipment (MTCTE) scheme via a Gazette notification 
dated 24.05.2022 , implying that mobile phones are no longer subject to mandatory testing for 
compliance with security standards under this framework. Also, the issue of White Labelling 
and import of telecom equipment from land border countries has been noted. The Committee 
observes that these gaps in the current regulatory framework need to be addressed and 
observes the Department may deliberate an d discuss these issues with concerned 
stakeholders to find a way for stricter enforcement mechanisms on these issues to ensure 
compliance with security standards and safeguard national interests. 
4.27 On the aspect of need to incorporate / mandate Zero Trust  Architecture (ZTA), the 
Department of Telecom has submitted the clarification that ZTA mandates strict identity 
verification and least -privilege access to prevent unauthorized access and lateral movement 
within networks, and is already incorporated as a r equirement under the Indian Telecom 
Security Assurance Requirements (ITSARs) framed by the National Centre for 
Communication Security (NCCS). Also, the ComSec Scheme's testing is based on these 
ITSARs, indicating that ZTA is effectively mandated and implem ented within the existing 
telecom security framework. The Committee notes the clarification given.

The Comm ittee observes that the current definition in Rule 2(1)(g) is broad, 
encompassing both service providers and network operators, which risks inconsistent 
application. The Committee recommends that suitable necessary action in this regard be 
taken by the Department of Telecom. 
          Para 4 (4.3) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Department should explicitly define the categories 
of data permissible for collection, limiting it to what is strictly necessary for telecom 
cybersecurity.  
         Para 4 (4.4) 
 
The Committee observes that telecommunication entities, as network operators, and 
users, as end -points, play a vital role in implementing corrective measures, justifying 
their inclusion in the data -sharing framework. The Committee recommends that a 
mechanism of having a periodic review of the data -sharing framework to assess its 
effectiveness in enhancing telecom cybersecurity and address emerging privacy or 
security challenges be set up. Besides efforts towards regular engagement with 
stakeholders regarding the sharing process and evolving cybersecurity standards shall 
also be beneficial. 
          Para 4 (4.5) 
 
The Committee is of the view that the phrase "adequate safeguards" is vague and fails 
to elaborate upon what level of safeguards will be consider ed adequate. Thus, the 
Committee recommends that to provide clarity on the term "adequate safeguards”, the 
Department should issue detailed guidelines specifying mandatory technical and 
procedural measures for authorised agencies and telecom entities.  
          Para 4 (4.6) 
 
The Committee recommends that to address concerns about the broadness of the term 
"fraudulent" and risks to innocent senders, the DoT may take necessary action to 
explicitly define the term, establish clear criteria and processes for d etermining 
fraudulence, and provide robust support for telecommunication entities and users in this 
regard.  
           Para 4 (4.7) 
 
The Committee observes that a standardized cybersecurity  policy is essential to address 
evolving threats and ensure that all entities, licensed or otherwise, maintain robust 
security practices. Thus, the Committee agrees with the laid requirement for all 
telecommunication entities to adopt a telecom cybersecuri ty policy, as it strengthens the 
security across a diverse ecosystem.  
          Para 4 (4.8) 
 
The Committee observes that framing clear guidelines on scope and frequency, by the 
DoT shall be helpful in ensuring that the cybersecurity objectives are readil y met by the 
TSPs.  
          Para 4 (4.9) 
 
25 

The Committee  recommends that inclusive stakeholder consultations be conducted so 
that a practical, secure, and effective log retention framework, which minimizes burden 
on telecommunication entities gets framed at the earliest.  
          Para 4 (4.10) 
 
The Committee observes that for cases requiring longer suspensions (e.g., complex 
investigations by law enforcement),  the DoT should allow extensions through a formal 
process, like clearly stating the reasons for such extension and also giving a tentative 
resolution timeline. 
          Para 4 (4.11) 
 
The Committee observes that to address concerns about unnecessary panic  and 
reputational loss of the telecommunication entity, the DoT should issue clear guidelines 
on disclosure circumstances, prioritize direct notifications to affected persons, and 
implement safeguards to protect privacy and manage public perception.  
         Para 4 (4.13) 
 
The Committee observes that the success of the portal shall depend on accessibility, 
security, and effective implementation. The Committee recommends that the portal’s 
development be expedited and all steps be taken to ensure that it is secure, user-friendly, 
and supported by clear guidelines.  
          Para 4 (4.14) 
 
The Committee recommends that suitable steps be taken towards enforcing malware 
testing, strengthening supply chain security, and promoting indigenous solutions, so that 
the country’s telecom networks can be safeguarded from malicious threats.  
          Para 4 (4.15) 
  
The Committee recommends that to secure telecom networks against quantum -based 
attacks, a strategic, phased adoption of Post-Quantum Cryptography ( PQC) should be 
implemented as its integration is essential to ensure long-term security. 
          Para 4 (4.16) 
 
The Committee observes that substandard spares could introduce vulnerabilities, 
compromising the integrity of critical infrastructure and thus mandating compliance for 
spares is a prudent measure to safeguard national security and public interest. However, 
the Committee also observes that smaller TSPs, in particular, may face challenges in 
sourcing compliant spares, especially if supply chains are limited or if compliant spares 
are costlier. Thus, while supporting the inclusion of spares  in the CTI Rules, 2024, as a 
critical security measure, the Committee recommends that the Department of Telecom 
may adopt a balanced approach through clear guidelines, phased implementation, and 
targeted support for smaller operators as these measures wil l strengthen the telecom 
infrastructure's resilience while fostering a conducive environment for compliance. 
          
Para 4 (4.17) 
 
The Committee is of the view that inspections enable proactive identification of 
vulnerabilities or non -compliance, and thereby reduces the risk of disruptions or 
cyberattacks on critical telecom infrastructure. Thus, the Committee endorses the 
inspection provisions under the Rules, as a critical mechanism to ensure compliance and 
security of telecom infrastructure. However, the Committee recommends that to 
enhance effectiveness and address concerns about operational disruptions, the DoT 
should adopt a hybr id inspection framework combining routine and incident -triggered 
inspections, supported by clear guidelines, standardized protocols, and stakeholder 
engagement.  
26 

The Committee feels that these measures will strengthen the security of CTI while 
fostering a collaborative and efficient compliance environment for telecom entities. 
            
 Para 4 (4.18) 
 
The Committee understands that logs are indispensable for post -incident analysis and 
that real -time access would be helpful in preventing or mitigating large-scale cyber 
incidents; however, the Committee also notes that continuous log submission may 
undermine the proactive monitoring capabilities leading to delays in the detection of 
emerging threats and a balanced approach needs to be developed. Taking n ote of the 
requirements of real-time log submission, the Committee recommends all steps be taken 
to ensure that the SOC infrastructure can handle large volumes of logs without 
compromising performance or security. Also, all steps to ensure that SOC infrastructure 
is fortified against cyberattacks through regular security assessments and compliance 
with global cybersecurity standards be taken. 
          Para 4 (4.19) 
 
The Committee appreciates the approach and the clarification given and observes that 
since Telecom operators possess detailed knowledge of their infrastructure, including its 
technical specifications, operational significance, and vulnerabilities, finalizing the CTI 
list in consultation with respective operators is both a practical and strategic necessity. 
           
Para 4 (4.20) 
 
The Committee endorses the requirement under Rule 7(1)( e), to maintain supply chain 
records as a critical measure to ensure the security of critical telecom infrastructure; 
however, to reduce the compliance burden on TSPs and enhance efficiency, the 
Committee recommends that DoT should make efforts to integrat e NSDTS data and 
adopt a phased approach for legacy equipment, and also provide robust support to 
TSPs. in case they face any issue in providing the data sought.  
          Para 4 (4.21) 
 
The Committee recommends that to improve practicality and reduce the  compliance 
burden, the DoT may consider aligning the reporting timeline with CERT -In’s 
“awareness” trigger, streamline reporting processes to avoid duplication, and provide 
robust support to TSPs. The Committee also notes that this shall bring similarity in 
provisions in both the Rules.  
          Para 4 (4.22) 
 
The Committee observes that without a precise definition, there is a risk of ambiguity, 
potentially allowing non -routine or significant updates to be misclassified as routine, 
bypassing necessary oversight, or causing confusion among Telecom Service Providers 
(TSPs) and OEMs about compliance requirements. Thus, the Committee recommends 
that in order to address concerns about ambiguity, the DoT should clarify and clearly 
define "routine software upd ate,” with defined criteria and guidelines so that TSPs and 
OEMs stand in compliance. 
          Para 4 (4.23) 
 
The Committee observes that though the Critical Telecom Infrastructure and Telecom 
Cyber Security Rules, 2024, provide a robust framework to addr ess these concerns, but 
targeted actions are needed to mitigate the specific risks posed by foreign, particularly 
Chinese-made, equipment.  
27 

The Committee recommends that to address the security risks associated with such 
telecom equipment, a phased "Rip -and-Replace" strategy should be implemented. 
Further this strategy could involve systematically identifying, removing, and replacing 
high-risk equipment with trusted, preferably indigenous, alternatives while 
strengthening supply chain security and enforcement mechanisms. This shall also allow 
India to position itself as a global leader in secure telecom manufacturing.  
          Para 4 (4.24) 
 
The Committee observes that there are instances where in some countries, regulators 
provide financial compensation or cost -sharing mechanisms to TSPs for compliance 
with national security -related infrastructure mandates. In view of the foregoing, the 
Committee recommends that the Government may assess the actual cost implications of 
these Rules and if required, may consider a hybrid approach in this regard or may 
consider offering incentives, such as tax breaks or subsidies, for compliance costs 
specifically tied to new mandates under the Rules. 
          Para 4 (4.25) 
 
The Committee observes that these gaps in the current regulatory framework need to be 
addressed and observes that the Department may deliberate and discuss these issues 
with concerned stakeholders to find a way for stricter enforcement mechanisms on these 
issues to ensure compliance with security standards and safeguard national interests.

5.   Thereafter, the Committee invited the Secretary and other Officials from the 
Department of Telecommunications to hear their submissions on the Telecommunications 
(Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 2024, and, the Telecommunications 
(Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024 formulated under the Telecommunications Act, 2023. 
The Chairman welcomed the Secretary and other officers from the Ministry and asked them to 
explain the salient features of these Rules and point out the manner in which the rules aim to 
secure critical telecom infrastructure through stringent compliance measures, penalties, and 
security directives, and also strengthen cyber security frameworks via mandatory audits, 
compliance protocols, and enforcement mechanisms. It was also asked that, the Committee be 
also provided, insights into the objectives, key provisions, operational scope, benefits, 
challenges, and stakeholder responses to these rules. 
30 

6. Secretary, Department of Telecommunications and other Officers in their submissions 
mentioned that the  Rules, which are under examination by the Committee, form the backbone 
of cyber telecom security and the world over, telecom has become the basic platform for 
providing any service, innovation, economic development, security or defence and   it is 
incumbent upon the Government and the private sector to ensure that both the players play 
their respective roles to ensure that adversaries do not gain control of these networks. The 
Secretary further informed that recently, the Government, recognizing the impo rtance of 
cyber security, modified the Allocation of Business Rules into three parts where the original 
cyber security remained with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the 
cyber security of telecom networks was specifically allocate d to Department of Telecom and 
prosecution and punishment on cybercrimes to the Ministry of Home Affairs.  
7. With the aid of power point presentation, various aspects of the critical telecom 
infrastructure Rules, 2023 were explained to the Committee.   The Ministry Officials 
informed that there were no telecom sector specific rules for critical infrastructure were in 
existence earlier and rules under the IT Act of 2000 were governing them.   The difference 
from the existing rules is that they are more speci fic to telecom sector and more 
comprehensive and cover the security standards and upgradation processes of telecom 
infrastructure which is declared as critical. This will ensure better monitoring of cyber 
security incidents that take place in telecom infra structure and mitigation measures taken 
timely. Rules have been framed under Section 22(4) of the Telecommunications Act which 
provides for standards, security practices, upgradation requirements and procedures to be 
implemented for the critical telecom in frastructure.  Two organisations in the DoT will 
specify the standards, the Telecommunication Engineering Centre and the National Centre for 
Communication Security, Bangalore. The salient features of the Rules, details about the 
consultations made with stakeholders and the response of the Government on the points raised 
etc were explained to the Committee.  
8.  On the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024, the Ministry explained that one of the 
objectives in the Statement of Objects and Reasons was, “Provision s for national security, 
public emergency and public safety” and rules were framed focusing on this.   Under section 
22 (2),  the measures may include collection, analysis and dissemination of traffic data that is 
generated, transmitted, received or stored in telecommunication networks.  These Rules were 
notified on 21 st November, 2024. The Ministry explained that there are two important 
stakeholders on which these Rules are applicable, viz    the telecommunication entities which 
provide telecommunication services or networks, and the users, who are involved in misuse of 
telecommunication resources for fraud, cheating, etc.  
31 

The Ministry further informed that before these rules were published, they went through an 
extensive round of public consultation and submissions from most of the associations of 
telecom service providers, several law firms and some public sector entities were received and 
all of them were considered and the rules were framed accordingly. Detailed submission on 
the rule-wise features was also done. It was submitted that t hese Rules establish a robust legal 
and operational framework for telecom security, ensuring compliance, accountability, and 
resilience against emerging cyber threats. 
9.  During the deliberations, several key points and queries were raised by Chairman and 
Members regarding the Telecom Cyber Security Rules and Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure Rules. The interconnected nature of both rules was pointed out and the need for 
proactive measures to address the rapid adv ancements in technology and cybersecurity was 
emphasized. Issues relating to inter -ministerial coordination, particularly between the 
Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Electronics and Information 
Technology (MeitY), Ministry of Home Affai rs (MHA), and other relevant departments, to 
ensure effective collaboration in enforcing these rules was discussed. The Chairman also 
sought information regarding the security of smartphones and apps, particularly those 
manufactured in other countries and also about the testing and enforcement mechanism to 
ensure that devices entering the Indian market are free from malware or spyware. Members of 
the Committee, raised concerns about cybercrime awareness, particularly in rural areas, and 
suggested leveraging  government platforms like UPI, Aadhaar, and banking portals to 
disseminate cybersecurity awareness messages.  Queries also touched upon the need for better 
coordination with state governments and cyber police, particularly in addressing financial 
frauds targeting vulnerable groups like senior citizens.  The Chairman also asked the Ministry 
to furnish the replies to the queries raised by the Members, in writing, within a week. 
10. The meeting was adjourned at 4.40 pm. A verbatim record of the proceedings was kept.

NOTIFICATION 
New Delhi, the 22nd November, 2024 
 G.S.R. 723(E).—Whereas a draft of the Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) 
Rules, 2024, which the Central Government proposes to make in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (4) of 
section 22 read with clause (w) of sub-section (2) of section 56 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 (44 of 2023), was 
published as required by sub -section (1) of  section 56 of the said Act vide notification of the Government of India in 
the Ministry of Communications, Department of Telecommunications numbe r G.S.R. 521(E), dated the 28th August, 
2024, in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, section 3, sub -section (i), dated the 28th August, 2024, inviting 
objections and suggestions from the persons likely to be affected thereby, before the expiry of  the period of thirty days 
from the date on which the copies of the Official Gazette containing the said notification were made available to the 
public; 
 And whereas copies of the said Official Gazette were made available to the public on the 29 th August, 2024; 
 And whereas the objections and suggestions received from the public in respect of the said draft rules have 
been duly considered by the Central Government; 
 Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (4) of section 22 read with clause (w) of 
sub-section (2) of section 56 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 (44 of 2023), the Central Government hereby makes 
the following rules, namely:- 
1. Short title and commencement.  – (1) These rules may be called the Telecommunications (Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 2024. 
 (2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.

2. Definitions. – (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires,– 
(a) “Act” means the Telecommunications Act, 2023 (44 of 2023); 
(b) “Chief Telecommunication Security Officer” means the Chief Telecommunication Security Officer 
appointed under rule 6 of the Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024;  
(c) “Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure” means any telecommunication network, or part thereof, 
notified under sub-section (3) of section 22 of the Act; 
(d) “portal” means the portal notified by the Central Government under sub-rule(1) of rule 10;  
(e) “security incident” shall have the same meaning assigned to it in clause (f) of sub -rule (1) of rule 2 of the  
Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024; and 
(f) “telecommunication entity” shall have the same meaning assigned to it in clause (g) of sub -rule (1) of rule 
2 of the Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024.   
(2) Words and expressions used in these rules and not defined herein but defined in the Act, shall have the 
meanings respectively assigned to them in the Act. 
3. Application. – (1) These rules shall apply to telecommunication network, or any part thereof, which has been 
notified by the Central Government as Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure under sub -section (3) of section 
22 of the Act, based on an assessment that disruption of s uch infrastructure shall have a debilitating impact on 
national security, economy, public health or safety of the nation. 
(2) The Central Government shall specify on the portal the form and manner in which every telecommunication 
entity shall provide the details of its telecommunication network, telecommunication services, and elements of such 
network and services.  
4. Compliance requirements. - Every telecommunication entity shall ensure that Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure, including any spares, hardware and software used in such Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, 
are in compliance with the following standards, namely:–   
(a) Essential Requirements (ERs), Interface Requirements (IRs), Indian Telecommunication Security Assurance 
Requirements (ITSARs) and specifications, testing requirements, or conformity assessment, as applicable, 
issued by Telecommunication Engineering Centre, National Centre for Communication Security, or any other 
person as may be notified by the Central Government for this purpose:  
 Provided that in the absence of such standards, a telecommunication entity may utilise only such Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure, including any spares, hardware and software used in such Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure, which meet the relevant standards as may be notified by the Central Government in 
this regard; 
(b) National Security Directive on Telecommunication Sector (NSDTS) as issued by the Central Government;  
(c) directives on communication security certification issued by the Central Government; and     
(d) such other standards applicable to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, as may be notified by the Central 
Government from time to time. 
5. Inspection of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure.  – (1) The Central Government, may, by an order, 
authorise its personnel to access and inspect hardware, software and data pertaining to Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure of telecommunication entities. 
(2)  Every telecommunication entity shall ensure access to any personnel authorised by the Central Government 
under sub-rule (1) for inspection of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure.  
6. Chief Telecommunication Security Officer.  – (1) The Chief Telecom Security Officer shall be responsible for 
the implementation of these rules.  
(2) The Central Government shall specify on the portal, the form and manner in which every telecommunication 
entity shall provide the details in respect of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, including the following details, 
namely:– 
(a) telecommunication network architecture of the Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure;  
(b) authorised personnel having access to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure;  
(c) inventory of hardware, software and spares related to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure;  
50

8  THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY    [PART II—SEC. 3(i)] 
 
(d) details of vulnerability, threat or risk analysis for the cyber security architecture of Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure; 
(e) Cyber Crisis Management Plan for Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure;  
(f) security audit reports and audit compliance reports of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure; 
(g) Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of services pertaining to Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure; 
(h) all logs relating to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure to assist in detection of anomalies and 
enable the Central Government to generate intelligence on real time basis; and  
(i) reporting of security incidents within the timelines specified for Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure under rule 7. 
7. Obligations related to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure. – (1) Every telecommunication entity shall 
comply with the following obligations, namely:– 
(a) ensure security of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, including through compliance with the 
standards as provided under rule 4;  
(b) maintain a complete list of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure along with the software and 
hardware details, as well as the dependencies on such Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure;  
(c) preserve in a secure manner, for a minimum period of two years or such other period as may be 
determined by the Central Government, logs and documentation of the telecommunication network 
architecture of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, including  changes in such 
telecommunication network architecture;   
(d) plan, develop and maintain adequate verification practices and protocols applicable for all personnel 
authorised to have access to Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, and undertake periodic review 
of the same as directed by the Central Government;  
(e) maintain records of the supply chain of the telecommunication equipment and other equipment 
deployed in the Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure till such infrastructure is in use, and 
provide such records, as and when sought for by the Central Government; 
(f) ensure that vulnerability or threat or risk analysis for telecommunication network architecture of 
Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure is carried out annually  or in such intervals as may be  
directed by the Central Government ; 
(g) plan, develop, maintain and review processes required for Service Level Agreements (SLAs) entered 
into by the telecommunication entities with their vendors in relation to Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure;  
(h) plan, develop, maintain and review processes of taking regular backup of logs of networking and 
communication devices, servers, systems and services supporting the functioning of the Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure; 
(i) implement standard operating procedures for security incident response systems, including disaster 
recovery and business continuity; 
(j) implement mechanisms to ensure intimation of security incident(s) to the Central Government, no 
later than six hours of occurrence of such incident, in the form and manner as may be specified on the 
portal; and 
(k) maintain a risk register including a graded risk assessment associated with different elements of 
Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure within its network, identifying the potential and severity 
of risks posed to the Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure and solutions to mitigate the same and 
produce such information as and when sought for by the Central Government .  
(2) Where a telecommunication entity requires remote access to its Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure for 
the purpose of repair or maintenance from a location outside of the territory of India, it shall do so only from such 
location for which it has obtained prior written approval from the Central Government, and it shall, for each instance of 
such remote access – 
(a) provide due intimation of such remote access to the Central Government in the form and manner specified on 
the portal; and 
51

[भाग II—खण् ड 3(i)] भारत का रािपत्र : असाधारण  9 
 
(b) ensure that the logs for such remote access are preserved for at least one year and provided as and when sought 
for by the Central Government. 
 
(3) Every telecommunication entity shall furnish a detailed report relating to the action taken by it under sub-rule (1) in 
the form and manner as may be specified on the portal.  
(4) The Central Government may, pursuant to any report or other information received from a telecommunication entity 
under sub-rule (3),–– 
(a)  seek further clarifications from such telecommunication entity; or  
(b)  issue any directions, orders or instructions to such telecommunication entity for the protection of Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure or mitigating risks to such infrastructure.  
8. Requirements for upgradation of Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure.  – (1) Where upgradation of the 
software or hardware of equipment which form part of the Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure  is required, 
the telecommunication entity shall make an application to the Central Government, along with details of the test 
reports for such upgradation and other relevant information in the form and manner as may be specified on the 
portal by that Government.      
(2) The Central Government shall, within fourteen days of receipt of the application under sub -rule (1),–   
(a) seek any further clarifications if required from the telecommunication entity;  
(b) issue directions to such entity to conduct further testing under sub-rule (3); or 
(c) approve or reject the application for upgradation activity. 
(3) The Central Government may direct a telecommunication entity to test any upgradation in the Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure in an appropriate controlled environment and submit the results of such tests in the 
form and manner, as may be specified by the Central Government on case to case basis, and the telecommunication 
entity shall comply with such directions. 
(4) Where the Central Government does not seek any clarification or issue directions or specify its approval or 
rejection under sub -rule (2) within a period of fourteen days from the date of receipt of such application, the 
telecommunication entity may proceed with such upgradation activity: 
 Provided that where the Central Government has sought clarifications under sub -rule (2), such time period of 
fourteen days shall be considered from the date of submission of clarification by such telecommunication entity:  
 Provided further that where the Central Government has directed to  test the upgradation under sub -rule (3), 
such time period of fourteen days shall be considered from the date of submission of the results of such tests in the form 
and manner as may be specified by the Central Government on case to case basis through secure mode. 
(5) Where upgradation is necessary for addressing or mitigating the adverse effects of a security incident, a 
telecommunication entity may undertake immediate upgradation in the software or hardware of any equipment that 
forms part of Critical Telecommunic ation Infrastructure without making an application under sub rule (1) and  within 
twenty-four hours of such upgradation, report to the Central Government in the form and manner as may be determined 
by the Central Government, with relevant details of – 
(a) the description of the concerned security incident; and 
(b) the relevant software or hardware of an equipment requiring upgradation and the nature of upgradation 
undertaken in respect of such equipment. 
(6) The Central Government may, upon receipt of information under sub -rule (5), seek further information or 
clarifications from the telecommunication entity, or issue directions for further testing and reporting, as it may consider 
necessary. 
(7) The telecommunication entity shall ensure preservation of records and information in relation to any 
upgradation, till such time the relevant Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure is in use, and such records shall be 
produced as and when sought by the Central Government.  
(8) Nothing in this rule shall apply to a routine software update aimed to incrementally improve performance or 
security of Critical Telecom Infrastructure. 
9. Contravention of rules. — Save as otherwise provided, any contravention of the provisions of these rules shall be 
dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

10. Digital implementation.  – (1) The Central Government shall notify a portal for the purpose of digital 
implementation of these rules and may also specify any other implementing mechanism.  
(2) Where the Central Government considers  it necessary to use any secure mode of communication, other than 
through the portal, for the issuance of any orders, directions or instructions to telecommunication entities, or for 
collection of any information from such telecommunication entities, it may use such secure mode of communication on 
case to case basis. 
(3) Every telecommunication entity shall ensure compliance with the obligations relating to reporting or 
submission of information to the Central Government under these rules using the portal or through a secure mode of 
communication as determined by the Central Government.
